source: KDT8 ch5; GG14 ch1; GG14 ch8

cards.front: What are the aims, subjects and dose strategy of a phase I trial?
cards.back: First-in-human study of safety, tolerability and human PK. Subjects are mostly healthy volunteers; when the drug is expected to be toxic (e.g. cancer or AIDS therapy) volunteer patients are used instead. Size: about 20 to 80 subjects (KDT); 10 to 100 (GG14); 20 to 100 (Katzung). Done by trained clinical pharmacologists with vital functions monitored and resuscitation at hand. Subjects receive the drug one by one, starting at about 1/100 to 1/10 of the highest dose that was non-toxic in animals, escalated stepwise to find the dose range for later study. Open label (no blinding).

cards.front: What does a phase II trial aim to establish?
cards.back: Therapeutic exploration and dose ranging: the first study in patients with the target disease ('proof of concept'). Size: about 100 to 500 patients (KDT); 50 to 500 (GG14); 100 to 200 (Katzung). Patients are selected by inclusion and exclusion criteria. Aims: therapeutic efficacy, dose range and ceiling effect; tolerability and PK are extended from phase I. Mostly controlled and randomised, blinded or open, generally at 2 to 4 centres. A candidate drug may be dropped here if efficacy is inadequate.

cards.front: What is a phase III trial, and what does its completion lead to?
cards.back: Therapeutic confirmation: randomised, usually double-blind comparison with existing therapy, done at many centres by specialists in the disease. Size: about 500 to 3000 patients (KDT); a few hundred to a few thousand (GG14); usually thousands (Katzung). It confirms efficacy, assesses safety on a wider scale, finalises indications and may add PK data. Some immunologically mediated toxicities first appear here. Completion leads to the marketing application: NDA, or BLA for biologics. Toxic but valuable drugs may receive restricted marketing permission (e.g. hospital use only).

cards.front: Classify: phases of a drug trial
cards.text: Phase {{I}} is the first-in-human study in about {{20 to 80}} subjects, usually {{healthy volunteers}}, and open label; phase {{II}} explores dose and efficacy in about 100 to 500 patients; phase {{III}} is a {{randomised, double-blind}} multicentre comparison in about 500 to 3000 patients that supports the marketing application; phase {{IV}} is {{postmarketing}} surveillance.

cards.front: Short note: Phase I clinical trials

points: Human pharmacology and safety: first human administration of the drug, run by a qualified clinical pharmacologist
Clinical studies are conventionally divided into 4 phases (KDT8)
Phase 0 microdosing, where done, comes before phase I

cards.front: What preclinical tests precede human trials?
cards.back: Animal work checks the whole pharmacological profile: screening, isolated organ and culture tests, disease models, systemic pharmacology, dose-response, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity in at least two species (one rodent, one non-rodent). Toxicity tests are acute (LD50, 1 to 3 days), subacute (2 to 12 weeks), chronic (6 to 12 months), reproduction and teratogenicity, mutagenicity (Ames test), and carcinogenicity. Toxicity work follows Good Laboratory Practices (GLP).

cards.front: Short note: Phase 0 (microdosing) study

points: Exploratory human study run before phase I
Uses sub-pharmacological doses in a few healthy volunteers
Dose about 1/100 of the estimated human dose, with a total of no more than about 100 micrograms
Drug measured with very sensitive methods: accelerator mass spectrometry (radiolabelled drug) or LC-MS/MS
Early human pharmacokinetic data
May replace some animal PK work and stop drugs that would fail on PK grounds before phase I
Helps choose the starting dose for phase I
Microdose PK may differ from PK at pharmacological doses
Not yet fully standardised; neither established nor mandatory

cards.front: What do phase IV studies detect that earlier phases cannot?
cards.back: Postmarketing studies in the general treated population, with far larger numbers and everyday prescribing. They pick up uncommon or idiosyncratic adverse effects, effects of long-term use and unsuspected drug interactions, and show real patterns of use. They also study groups excluded from earlier trials (children, elderly, pregnant or lactating women, renal or hepatic disease), and new formulations, routes or fixed-dose combinations.

cards.front: Short note: Phase 0 (microdosing) trials

points: Microdosing study done before phase I, to cut the cost and time of development
Very low dose (about 1/100th of the estimated human dose, or a maximum of 100 microgram total) given to healthy volunteers
Pharmacokinetics measured with sensitive instruments
Microdose pharmacokinetics may differ from those at pharmacological doses

cards.front: Outline the stages of new drug development from molecule to market.
cards.back: Synthesis or isolation of the compound, then preclinical animal studies; if promising, the regulator issues an Investigational New Drug licence for clinical trials in phases I to III; after phase III a new drug application is filed for marketing; phase IV follows. Development takes at least 10 years and costs about 500 to 1000 million US dollars, and only a few of thousands of compounds reach man.

cards.front: Short note: Phases of clinical trials

points: Therapeutic exploration and dose ranging
About 100-500 patients chosen by inclusion and exclusion criteria; aims: efficacy, dose range and ceiling effect
Therapeutic confirmation and comparison
Usually multicentric; enlarges the base for regulatory and credibility needs
Phase 0 microdosing precedes phase I (see Phase 0 card)

cards.front: Why is randomisation used, and when is stratified randomisation chosen?
cards.back: Subjects are allocated by a preselected random number table or computer programme, so each has an equal chance of entering the test or control group. Neither investigator nor patient can influence allocation, so that source of bias is removed. When groups may end up ill-matched (especially small groups), stratified randomisation is used: subjects are first divided by age, sex, disease severity or other variables, and randomised within each stratum. Too many strata defeat the purpose.

cards.front: Short note: Randomization in clinical trials

points: Subjects allocated to test or control group by a random number table or computer programme
Every subject has an equal chance of either group
Removes investigator and subject bias in allocation
Stratified randomization (age, sex, severity) if needed

cards.front: What is blinding in a clinical trial, and what is an open trial?
cards.back: Blinding hides which treatment (test or control) a person is getting. Single blind hides it from the subject; double blind hides it from both subject and investigator. The two medicines must look, weigh and taste alike and come in unlabelled packs numbered per patient. The allocation code is held by a third party (data management) not involved in treatment or recording, and is broken only after the trial ends. Why: it removes conscious and unconscious expectation bias. A trial where the treatment is not hidden is called open (not every trial needs blinding).

cards.front: What is a controlled trial, and what can the control group receive?
cards.back: A controlled trial has a comparator group as similar as possible to the test group, so any difference can be credited to the test drug. The control gets either a placebo (only if ethically permissible) or the existing standard treatment (active control). The regimen (dose, frequency, duration) is fixed in advance, so results apply only to that regimen; separate dose-ranging trials are needed to judge other doses.

cards.front: What are the advantages of a multicentric trial?
cards.back: Many large trials run at more than one centre, sometimes in several countries. Advantages: more patients recruited in less time; results apply to a wider population; regulatory requirements of several countries can be met; credibility of the trial rises. Phase III trials are usually multicentric.

cards.front: Compare parallel-group and crossover trial designs.
cards.back: Parallel: test and control groups run at the same time, each with different patients. Crossover: the same patients receive both treatments in a random order, so each serves as its own control. Crossover reduces between-patient variation and the sample size needed, but carry-over and order effects can occur, and it suits only chronic diseases that stay stable over time.

cards.front: What is an adaptive trial design?
cards.back: Conventional statistical methods may fail to give a clear answer when trials meet unexpected confounders, loss of subjects or marked subgroup differences. Adaptive statistical methods allow the study design to be changed when interim data show the need. They may permit decisions on superiority as well as non-inferiority, shorten the trial, reveal new benefits and give more reliable conclusions.

cards.front: Why does the Declaration of Helsinki discourage placebo controls when an effective treatment exists?
cards.back: If a proven alternative exists, subjects randomised to placebo would in effect be denied treatment during the trial, which is an ethical problem (beneficence, non-maleficence). So the comparator then should be the existing standard treatment (active control). This is also why a placebo is used only where ethically permissible.

cards.front: Short note: Role of placebo in clinical trials and therapy

points: Inert substance given in the guise of a medicine
Acts by psychodynamic, not pharmacodynamic, means and often gives responses like the active drug; some people are more suggestible
Serves as the control in a controlled trial, if ethically permissible
Otherwise the existing standard treatment is the active control
Opposite effect: negative response from patient pessimism or loss of faith in the drug or doctor
Can oppose the therapeutic effect of the active drug
Helsinki Declaration discourages placebo when an alternative treatment is available

cards.front: What is a sequential trial design, and when is it applicable?
cards.back: Matched pairs of subjects are compared one pair at a time and scored as A better than B, B better than A, or no difference. The score is plotted continuously until a preset boundary for superiority, inferiority or no difference is crossed, and then the trial stops. It uses the fewest subjects, but suits only drugs and diseases where clinical end points come quickly and matched pairs can be recruited.

cards.front: Short note: Bias in clinical trials and how it is minimised

points: Conscious and unconscious bias of investigators and subjects, for or against the test drug
Eliminating bias is the greatest challenge in a trial; credibility depends on it
Randomisation, stratified where groups may be unbalanced
Blinding: single (subject) or double (subject and investigator); identical-looking medicines in unlabelled packets; code held by a third party
Rigorous follow-up and outcome assessment; assessors unaware of treatment if full blinding is impossible
Proper control group: placebo if ethical, otherwise standard treatment
Inclusion and exclusion criteria fixed in advance
Primary and secondary end points and the statistical method pre-specified

cards.front: Short note: Meta-analysis

points: Pools data from several similar randomised controlled trials of the same drug or class on the same end point
Enlarges numbers, raising significance and power, and resolves discordant small trials
Selection bias in choosing trials
Publication bias: negative results less often published
Trials differ in methodology and conduct
Comprehensive literature search
Objective inclusion criteria
Only randomised trials of assured quality
Proper statistics for pooling
Supported beta-blockers in heart failure and statins to lower coronary artery disease risk

cards.front: Essay: Principles of controlled clinical trials

points: Clinical trial: prospective, ethically designed study in humans to discover, verify or compare therapeutic measures
Credibility depends on eliminating bias
Comparator group: placebo (if ethical) or active control
Parallel versus crossover; multicentric trials; sequential designs
Randomisation (stratified if needed)
Blinding: single, double, open trials; code held by a third party
Sample size fixed beforehand: significance, power, expected difference, variability
Interim analysis by an independent committee with early stopping
Independent ethics committee approval; written informed consent
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice
Randomised controlled double-blind trial is the most credible evidence of efficacy, safety or comparative value

cards.front: Classify: errors and power in a trial
cards.text: A type {{I}} error is a {{false positive}} result, declaring a difference that does not exist; a type {{II}} error is a {{false negative}}; the {{power}} of a trial is 1 minus the type II error rate.

cards.front: Why must sample size be calculated before a trial begins?
cards.back: Money and ethics both require the smallest number of subjects that can still give a valid answer: too few cannot settle the question, too many expose people needlessly. The trial uses only a sample of all patients, which may not represent the population, so results are never absolutely conclusive. Hence the number needed to show test better, control better, or no difference is calculated statistically in advance.

cards.front: What is the difference between a clinical end point and a surrogate end point?
cards.back: A clinical end point is an outcome that matters to the patient, such as myocardial infarction, fracture or death. A surrogate end point is an easily measured marker that is expected to predict it: LDL cholesterol for myocardial infarction, bone mineral density for fracture, HbA1c for diabetic complications. Surrogates cut trial cost and time, but the marker may not truly reflect the disease outcome.

cards.front: Recall: how sample size moves
cards.text: A {{smaller}} expected difference between groups needs a {{larger}} sample; higher power or a stricter significance level needs a {{larger}} sample; a more variable primary end point needs {{more}} subjects.

cards.front: Short note: Surrogate versus clinical endpoints

points: Clinical end point: patient-relevant outcome such as myocardial infarction, fracture or death
Surrogate end point: an easily measured marker thought to predict the clinical outcome, e.g. LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, bone mineral density, HbA1c, blood pressure
Trials are cheaper and quicker

Ezetimibe was approved on LDL lowering; ENHANCE then found no reduction in carotid intima-media thickness despite extra LDL lowering; the later IMPROVE-IT trial showed reduced MI and stroke with ezetimibe plus statin
Torcetrapib raised HDL but increased cardiovascular deaths
CAST: antiarrhythmics suppressed ventricular arrhythmias (the surrogate) but increased sudden cardiac death
Regulators are cautious about surrogate end points; the marker must truly reflect patient benefit

cards.front: What factors determine the sample size of a clinical trial?
cards.back: Four inputs: the significance level (type I error, usually 0.05); the power (1 minus type II error); the smallest clinically meaningful difference expected between groups; and the variability of the primary endpoint. A smaller expected difference, greater variability, higher power or a stricter significance level all increase the number needed. Sample size is calculated in advance because it must be minimal for both ethical and financial reasons.

cards.front: Short note: Interim analysis and early stopping of trials

points: Analysis of accumulating results at intervals while a large trial is still running
An independent committee, not the investigators
Early termination once a decisive result, positive or negative, is reached
Otherwise the trial continues
Unethical to keep giving remaining patients a treatment already shown to be inferior
Sequential trial: matched pairs scored continuously until a preset boundary of superiority, inferiority or no difference is reached; suits drugs whose end points are reached quickly

cards.front: What is a non-inferiority trial, and why would one be done?
cards.back: A trial designed to show that a new drug is not inferior to existing treatment, rather than better. It is worthwhile when the new drug may offer other advantages: tolerability, safety, convenience, cost, or use in a particular patient subgroup. Many phase II and III studies are designed this way. The sample size calculation differs depending on whether the aim is to show equivalence or non-inferiority, or a significant difference.

cards.front: Essay: Design of a non-inferiority phase III trial

points: Aim: show the new drug is not inferior to standard treatment
Justified by expected gains in tolerability, safety, convenience, cost or use in a subgroup
Randomised, parallel-group trial against the existing standard treatment (active control)
Double blind with identical-looking medicines where possible
Inclusion and exclusion criteria and the dosage regimen fixed in advance
Primary and secondary end points specified in advance
Surrogate end points only if they reliably reflect clinical benefit
Calculated beforehand from significance level, power, the clinically relevant difference and variability of response
Calculation depends on aiming for non-inferiority rather than a difference
Pre-specified statistical method
Interpretation is hard with confounders, loss of subjects or subgroup differences
Independent ethics committee approval and written informed consent
Interim analysis by an independent committee

cards.front: Case: a drug approved on LDL lowering later shows no effect on carotid thickness. What does this teach about surrogate end points?
cards.back: Ezetimibe lowers LDL further than a statin alone, and was approved assuming LDL is a good surrogate for myocardial infarction and stroke. The ENHANCE trial then found no extra reduction in carotid intima-media thickness with ezetimibe plus statin, so the surrogate was questioned (critics blamed the patient group). A 7-year trial of over 18,000 high-risk patients (IMPROVE-IT) later showed fewer myocardial infarctions and strokes, vindicating approval. Lesson: surrogates save time and money but their link to hard outcomes must be shown, sometimes only by a later clinical-end-point trial.

cards.front: Short note: Good Clinical Practice (GCP)

points: Standards laid down by the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) for trial design, ethics, conduct, monitoring, auditing, recording, analysis and reporting
Assures that data and reported results are credible and accurate
Protects the rights, integrity and confidentiality of trial subjects
Principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association)
National guidelines too: in India, ICMR ethical guidelines for biomedical research on human participants
Every trial needs prior approval by an independent ethics committee as per GCP

cards.front: Recall: who does what before and during a drug trial
cards.text: The {{sponsor}} files the {{IND}} application before human testing; an {{institutional review board}} at each site approves the plan; after phase III the sponsor applies for marketing by an {{NDA}} (or a BLA for biologics).

cards.front: What is the Declaration of Helsinki and how does it relate to GCP?
cards.back: It is the World Medical Association statement of ethical principles for research on human subjects. Good Clinical Practice, laid down by the ICH, gives standards for design, ethics, conduct, monitoring, auditing, recording, analysis and reporting of trials; following it assures credible, accurate data and protects the rights, integrity and confidentiality of subjects as set out in Helsinki. In India, ICMR (2006) also framed ethical guidelines for biomedical research on human participants.

cards.front: What are the roles of the sponsor, the investigators and the institutional review board in a drug trial?
cards.back: Sponsor (usually a pharmaceutical company): files the Investigational New Drug (IND) application describing preclinical data and the protocol before human testing, and applies for marketing (NDA or BLA) after phase III. Investigators: run the trial; in phase III they are usually specialists in the disease. Institutional review board (ethics committee) at each facility: an interdisciplinary body that must review and approve the scientific and ethical plan before testing in humans.

cards.front: Short note: Ethics committee in clinical trials

points: Independent body; every trial needs its scrutiny and approval as per GCP
Weighs safety and ethical issues as well as the scientific importance of the study
Autonomy: freedom, dignity and confidentiality; right to choose whether to join or continue
Beneficence: intent to do good to the subject or society
Non-maleficence: no harm or undue risk
Justice: fairness, honesty and impartiality in obtaining, analysing and reporting data
Interdisciplinary institutional review board at each trial facility

cards.front: Short note: Ethics committee for clinical trials under the NDCT Rules 2019

points: At least 7 members from medical, non-medical, scientific and non-scientific areas
At least one lay person, one woman, one legal expert, and one independent member (social scientist, NGO representative, philosopher, ethicist or theologian)
At least half not associated with the institution; chairperson unaffiliated; member secretary from the institution
Medical scientists and clinicians need postgraduate qualification; all members trained in GCP
Registered by the CLA; valid 5 years
Renewal applied for 90 days before expiry
Changes in membership intimated to the CLA within 30 days
At least 5 members, including a medical scientist (preferably a pharmacologist), a clinician, a legal expert, and a social scientist, NGO representative or lay person
Invited subject experts cannot vote
Protect rights, safety and well-being of subjects, with extra care for vulnerable groups (e.g. prisoners, students, the impoverished, minors)
Ongoing review; may revoke approval with recorded reasons
Report on SAEs with opinion on compensation
Schedule Y also required at least 7 members, but without the detailed composition rules

cards.front: Short note: Contract research organisation (CRO)

points: Company that takes on sponsor duties under contract as an independent contractor
Designs, selects, monitors and evaluates studies, and prepares regulatory submissions
After the 1962 Kefauver-Harris amendments, efficacy had to be proven before marketing
Companies outsourced non-critical studies to cut workload and cost
Turns fixed development costs into variable costs
Medical: trial protocol design and medical input
Regulatory submission team
Clinical operations: site selection, monitoring, study close-out
Data management: databases and clean data for analysis
Grew after the 2005 Schedule Y change allowed trials in India to run alongside other countries
Sponsors use CROs; India attractive for patient pool, hospitals and stability studies
Shortage of skilled staff such as CRAs, especially with international GCP experience

cards.front: How does an ethics committee categorise proposals for review?
cards.back: By risk. Expedited review is for research with minimal average risk, for example studies of drugs or devices that are already approved. Full review is for research with more than minimal risk. The member secretary screens each proposal for completeness and assigns the category.

cards.front: Case: a company outsources an Indian multicentre phase III trial. Who does what before the first patient is enrolled?
cards.back: The sponsor has filed the IND (and later applies by NDA); a CRO, if contracted, takes on sponsor duties such as designing, monitoring (CRAs), data management and regulatory submissions. An independent ethics committee at each site must scrutinise and approve the protocol (GCP), and under the NDCT Rules trial permission is also needed from the licensing authority. Investigators, usually disease specialists, then take written informed consent.

cards.front: Classify: components of valid informed consent
cards.text: Consent must be {{voluntary}}, informed and {{written}}; the subject keeps the right to decide whether to {{continue}} in the trial (autonomy).

cards.front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define a serious adverse event (SAE) in a clinical trial?
cards.back: An untoward medical occurrence during a clinical trial that results in death; in-patient hospitalisation (if the study was on out-patients) or prolonged hospitalisation (if on in-patients); persistent or significant disability or incapacity; a congenital anomaly or birth defect; or is otherwise life-threatening. The NDCT Rules amended the earlier Schedule Y rule (Rule 122DAB).

cards.front: Name the four ethical principles an ethics committee must ensure a trial does not breach.
cards.back: Autonomy (freedom, dignity, confidentiality; right to join or withdraw), beneficence (aim to do good to subject and society), non-maleficence (no harm or undue risk), justice (fairness, honesty and impartiality in obtaining, analysing and communicating data). Informed consent expresses autonomy; risk assessment expresses non-maleficence.

cards.front: What is informed consent and why is it required?
cards.back: Written, voluntary agreement of a subject after being told that the drug is investigational, the nature and risks of the trial, that allocation to test or control is random and unknown to them, and that they may refuse or leave at any time. It puts autonomy into practice and is needed before enrolment. Those who cannot consent (unconscious, demented, mentally ill) need special handling.

cards.front: What must trial subjects be told, and what are the limits of informed consent?
cards.back: Subjects must be told that the drug is investigational, the nature and risks of the trial, and that they may be randomly and unknowingly assigned to test or control. They must be free to decline, or to stop participating (autonomy), and confidentiality is protected. Consent is proper and written. Limits: unconscious, demented or mentally ill patients cannot consent, and trials in children and the elderly raise similar concerns, yet such groups still need trials.

cards.front: Recall: SAE reporting timelines under the NDCT Rules 2019
cards.text: The investigator reports every SAE to the CLA, the sponsor and the EC within {{24 hours}}. For SAE of death, the sponsor and investigator send analysed reports to the CLA and head of institution within {{14 days}}; the EC sends its report with an opinion on compensation within {{30 days}}; the expert committee recommends cause and compensation within {{60 days}}; the CLA decides compensation within {{90 days}}; the sponsor pays within {{30 days}} of the order.

cards.front: Short note: Medical management and compensation for trial injury under the NDCT Rules 2019

points: Sponsor gives free medical management for as long as required in the investigator's opinion, or until the injury is shown to be unrelated to the trial or BA/BE study
Payable for clinical trial-related injury or death
Quantum determined by the CLA using the formula in the Seventh Schedule
Paid by the sponsor or its representative
Investigator reports the SAE within 24 hours
EC forwards its analysed report with an opinion on compensation
CLA may constitute an independent expert committee, which recommends cause and quantum within 60 days
CLA passes the order within 90 days of the SAE report
Sponsor pays within 30 days of the order and submits payment details to the CLA

cards.front: Case: a trial participant dies of unclear cause. Trace the actions and compensation process in India.
cards.back: Investigator reports the SAE within 24 h to the licensing authority, sponsor and ethics committee. Sponsor and investigator send analysed reports within 14 days; the EC gives its report and opinion on compensation within 30 days. An expert committee may recommend cause and quantum within 60 days; the CLA orders compensation (Seventh Schedule formula) within 90 days; the sponsor pays within 30 days. Free medical management continues as needed for related injury.

cards.front: What is an orphan drug?
cards.back: A drug or biological product for diagnosis, treatment or prevention of a rare disease, or of a commoner disease endemic only in resource-poor areas, for which there is no reasonable expectation that development and marketing costs will be recovered from sales. Under the US Orphan Drug Amendment (1983), a rare disease affects fewer than 200,000 people in the USA. Governments offer tax benefits and other incentives. Examples given orphan status: clofazimine, paromomycin, sodium stibogluconate, rituximab, bortezomib.

cards.front: What is an academic clinical trial under the NDCT Rules 2019?
cards.back: A trial intended solely for academic research. It needs only Ethics Committee approval; no permission from the DCGI is required. Its results must not be used for promotional purposes or to seek regulatory approval.

cards.front: Under the NDCT Rules 2019, what counts as a new drug?
cards.back: A drug not used to any significant extent in India and not approved by the Central Licensing Authority (CLA) for its claims. It also includes an approved drug with new claims (indication, route, dose or dosage form), a new fixed-dose combination or changed ratio, and modified-release or novel delivery forms. Vaccines, rDNA products, monoclonal antibodies, stem-cell, gene-therapy products and xenografts are included too.

cards.front: Recall: NDCT trial approval timelines
cards.text: The CLA decides within {{90 days}} for drugs developed outside India and {{30 days}} for drugs developed in India; no reply means {{deemed approval}}. Permission is valid {{2 years}}, and a rejected applicant may seek reconsideration within {{60 days}}.

cards.front: Why do orphan drugs need special incentives?
cards.back: Proving safety and efficacy in small populations is complex; little basic research is done on rare diseases, so rational targets are few; and development cost weighs heavily when the target population is small. Excessive product-liability costs (e.g. failure-to-warn claims for rare harms not detected in small trials) are a further disincentive. Hence tax benefits and other incentives, and support from not-for-profit foundations.

cards.front: Short note: New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) Rules, 2019

points: In force from 25 March 2019 (the chapter on ethics committees for biomedical and health research from 21 September 2019)
Replaced Part XA and Schedule Y of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 (older texts, e.g. KDT8, still describe Schedule Y)
Apply to new drugs, investigational drugs, ethics committees, BA/BE studies and clinical trials
Not used in India to any significant extent and not approved by the Central Licensing Authority (CLA) for its claims
Also: approved drug with new claims (indication, route, dose, dosage form); new fixed-dose combination or changed ratio; modified-release or novel delivery form
Also: vaccines, rDNA products, monoclonal antibodies, stem-cell products, gene therapy products, xenografts; phytopharmaceutical drugs added
Decision within 90 days for drugs developed outside India, 30 days for new drugs developed in India; no reply means deemed approval
Trial permission valid 2 years
Rejected applicant may seek reconsideration within 60 days
Two types: for clinical trials and BA/BE studies, and for biomedical and health research
Registration valid 5 years
CLA (DCGI) informed of EC approval within 15 working days
6-monthly trial status report to DCGI through the SUGAM portal; enrolment status every 3 months
Termination notified to CLA within 30 days with reasons
Post-trial access to the drug free of cost, on investigator recommendation and EC approval
Academic trials need EC approval only

cards.front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define an orphan drug, and what concessions do they give?
cards.back: An orphan drug is one intended to treat a condition affecting not more than five lakh (500,000) persons in India. Concessions: fast-track approval and special status, including a complete fee waiver for clinical trial filing; expedited review where safety and efficacy evidence is established even before all trial phases are complete (post-marketing trials may then be required); and waiver of the local clinical study and phase IV if the CLA is satisfied. Marketing still needs CDSCO authorisation to import or manufacture.

cards.front: Why can orphan drugs be approved before all trial phases finish, and what safeguards remain?
cards.back: Small patient numbers make large trials hard and returns low, so rules give incentives (India: fee waiver, fast-track; see also tax benefits in the US). In India, where safety and efficacy evidence is already established, expedited review is allowed even if not all phases are done, but post-marketing trials may then be required to confirm the benefit. Local clinical study and phase IV may be waived only if the CLA is satisfied, and marketing still needs CDSCO authorisation.

cards.front: How is pharmacovigilance organised in India and internationally (as given in KDT)?
cards.back: Pharmacovigilance centres exist in most countries, with the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (Sweden) as the international collaborating centre. In India, CDSCO coordinates the pharmacovigilance programme, with peripheral, regional and zonal monitoring centres and a National Pharmacovigilance Advisory Committee. Centres collect, communicate and disseminate ADR data by linking with hospitals and practitioners, and assess causality (Naranjo algorithm) and severity (modified Hartwig scale).

cards.front: Classify: observational designs in pharmacovigilance
cards.text: A {{cohort}} study follows users and non-users of a drug to find uncommon adverse effects; a {{case-control}} study compares the frequency of drug use in cases with an adverse response against controls.

cards.front: Define adverse effect, adverse drug reaction (ADR) and adverse drug event (ADE).
cards.back: Adverse effect: any undesirable or unintended consequence of drug use, trivial or serious. ADR: a noxious change suspected to be due to a drug, at normal doses, needing treatment, dose reduction or caution in future use; it excludes trivial or expected effects and poisoning. ADE: any untoward medical occurrence during treatment, not necessarily caused by the drug; all events are recorded first and causality is judged later on pooled data.

cards.front: How is causality of an adverse event assessed?
cards.back: Four criteria: temporal relationship (does timing fit drug exposure), previous knowledge (known to cause it before), dechallenge (event subsides on stopping) and rechallenge (event recurs on re-giving; often unethical so not done). Grades: definite, probable, possible, doubtful. Centres use the Naranjo algorithm for causality and the modified Hartwig scale for severity.

cards.front: Why can spontaneous adverse-event reports not give the true incidence of a drug reaction?
cards.back: The denominator is unknown, because the number of patients exposed to the drug is not recorded. The numerator is also incomplete: most reactions go unreported, reporting patterns change over the life of the product, and reports often lack dose, concomitant drugs or outcome. Media attention and litigation further distort reporting, so reports cannot be used to compare rates between drugs.

cards.front: What is a safety signal and how is it detected?
cards.back: A signal is a possible link between a drug and an adverse event that needs evaluation. Signals are found by disproportionality analysis, which compares how often an event is reported with the drug against its frequency across the whole database. These methods need no drug-use denominator but rely on assumptions that are hard to verify, so a signal almost always needs confirmation from controlled studies.

cards.front: When is a single case report strong evidence that a drug caused an event?
cards.back: When the event is rare or unlikely from other causes, appears close in time after exposure, has few other risk factors, and the drug carries a large excess risk. Examples are anaphylaxis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and rhabdomyolysis with cerivastatin. Otherwise a case report only raises suspicion.

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI)

points: 1989: six regional ADR centres
1997: India joined the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring (Uppsala Monitoring Centre)
2004: National Pharmacovigilance Programme
14 July 2010: PvPI launched with AIIMS, New Delhi as National Coordination Centre (NCC)
15 April 2011: NCC shifted to the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), Ghaziabad
Conducted by CDSCO (Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare); coordinated by IPC as NCC
ADR Monitoring Centres (AMCs), mostly in medical colleges, send reports to the NCC through VigiFlow
Data go to the WHO-UMC global database; CDSCO takes regulatory decisions on NCC recommendations
Suspected ADR reporting form (voluntary, by healthcare professionals)
Report all suspected reactions to new drugs, all suspected interactions, and serious reactions (death, life-threatening, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly)
KDT8 describes the older CDSCO-coordinated programme with peripheral, regional and zonal centres

cards.front: Essay: From a suspected adverse drug reaction to regulatory action

points: Premarketing trials are too small to detect rare ADRs; safety knowledge evolves over the drug's life cycle
Spontaneous reports (e.g. FAERS via MedWatch in the US; CDSCO-coordinated programme in India)
Published case reports
Observational cohort and case-control studies
Postmarketing clinical trials
Disproportionality methods on the spontaneous report database
Causality judged by temporal relation, previous knowledge, dechallenge and rechallenge; Naranjo algorithm
Denominator unknown
Heavy underreporting
Incomplete reports; confounding in observational studies
Safety communication and label change, including boxed warning
Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS)
Withdrawal from the market

cards.front: Is a phase IV trial the same as post-marketing surveillance?
cards.back: No. Phase IV trials test the drug in real-life use: factors that change its effect, long-term and rare effects, special populations, and interactions. The CLA may require them or the sponsor may start them. Post-marketing surveillance (PMS), also called a non-interventional or observational study, is active surveillance run under the conditions of the approved package insert. Its protocol needs CLA approval, and PMS is mandatory for a new drug.

cards.front: How often must the PSUR be filed after a new drug is approved, and how long does new-drug status last?
cards.back: The marketing authorisation holder files a periodic safety update report every 6 months for the first 2 years, then yearly for the next 2 years. The drug keeps new-drug status for 4 years.

cards.front: Which studies, besides phase IV, can be run in the post-marketing period?
cards.back: Non-interventional (observational) studies, post-marketing surveillance, adverse drug monitoring, case-control studies of ADRs, drug utilisation studies and observational registries. Together they track real-world safety and use after the drug is on the market.

cards.front: What is a controlled human infection model (CHIM)?
cards.back: Healthy volunteers are deliberately infected with a pathogen so that a candidate vaccine or drug can be tested for preliminary efficacy.

cards.front: Short note: Controlled human infection model (CHIM)

points: Healthy participants are deliberately infected with the pathogen
Called phase IIa challenge studies
Preliminary efficacy of vaccine candidates against malaria, typhoid and cholera
Only for selected diseases where it is scientifically and ethically justified
Pathogen must not cause lethal disease, and cure must be achievable
Vaccines go to healthy people, so the safety margin must be very high
Phase II and III vaccine trials are field studies with cold-chain problems

cards.front: Essay: Phase II trial of a new antihypertensive agent

points: Phase I data on safety, pharmacokinetics and dose range in healthy volunteers
Animal toxicity studies and an investigational licence from the regulator before first human dosing
Independent ethics committee approval and written informed consent
Patients picked by inclusion and exclusion criteria, fixed in advance
Controlled and randomised; may be single-blind, double-blind or open
Dose, frequency and duration fixed in advance; usually 2-4 centres (KDT8)
Katzung describes a single-blind design with placebo and an active control
KDT8: 100-500 patients; Katzung: 100-200; Padmaja: 100-300. Quote the range the book in use gives
Efficacy: fall in blood pressure as a surrogate marker, linked to outcomes where possible
Tolerability and pharmacokinetics studied alongside
Primary and secondary end points set before the trial starts
Establish efficacy, dose range and ceiling effect
Drug may be dropped here if efficacy is inadequate
Only about 25% of innovative drugs move from phase 2 to phase 3 (Katzung)

cards.front: What is an exploratory therapeutic trial (phase II type)?
cards.back: A study in patients with the target disease to show efficacy (proof of concept), define the dose range and ceiling effect, with tolerability and pharmacokinetics as an extension of phase I.

cards.front: What is a 2 x 2 factorial trial design?
cards.back: Subjects are randomised to one of four groups: A alone, B alone, A plus B, or neither (placebo). Two treatments are tested with one set of subjects, and the interaction of A with B can be examined.

cards.front: Short note: Factorial design in clinical trials

points: Two or more treatments tested together in all combinations
2 x 2 example: A alone, B alone, A + B, placebo
Larger designs such as 2 x 3 are analysed by multifactor ANOVA (Medhi)
Efficient use of subjects: two treatments evaluated with the same number of individuals
Examines whether A and B interact
Medhi: 2 x 3 design of treatment type against high or low fat diet on hypertension symptoms

cards.front: Short note: Adaptive clinical trial designs

points: Pre-planned flexibility to change trial parameters at interim analysis
Example: adjusting the sample size
Needs statistical methods that allow the design to change when interim data show the need (Katzung)
Adaptive dose-finding: finds minimum effective or maximum tolerable dose, often Bayesian
Biomarker-adaptive: picks a responsive subgroup and can add or drop arms
Treatment-switching and adaptive-hypothesis designs (e.g. superiority changed to non-inferiority)
Group-sequential, drop-the-losers, seamless and multiple combinations
Ethically better: fewer patients may be needed
Useful in exploratory, dose-finding and confirmatory phases
Can shorten the trial and give more reliable conclusions (Katzung)
Regulator must be convinced in advance
Modelling and simulation needed before starting
Costlier and harder to plan and run than a conventional design

cards.front: Define pharmacoepidemiology.
cards.back: The study of how drugs are used, and of their effects and side effects, in a well-defined population. Observational epidemiological studies support safety signals but cannot alone prove cause and effect.

cards.front: What are the four dimensions of quality of life used in drug evaluation?
cards.back: Physical mobility; freedom from pain and distress; capacity for self-care; ability to engage in normal work and social interaction. It is measured by questionnaire on the subject's own perceived health.

cards.front: Short note: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in drug evaluation

points: Life years alone miss quality: a longer life can be of low quality
Economists combine quantity and quality into the quality-adjusted life year (QALY)
Questionnaire on the patient's perceived health
Four dimensions: physical mobility, freedom from pain and distress, self-care, normal work and social life
Benefit-risk judgement for the individual and for society
Cost-effectiveness appraisal, e.g. NICE in the UK
Resource allocation between patient groups
Quality is harder to measure than quantity

cards.front: What is the Clinical Trial Registry of India (CTRI)?
cards.back: A registry set up jointly by ICMR, DST and WHO to make drug trials transparent and accountable. Registered details are freely accessible to the public.

cards.front: Short note: Clinical trial registry (CTRI)

points: Makes drug development transparent and accountable
Gives doctors and the public information on new drugs and trials
Joint effort of ICMR, DST and WHO
All clinical trials conducted in India should be registered
Registration is needed before trial data can be published
Registered details are open to everyone
Conflict in source: Padmaja also calls registration voluntary and free, while stating that all trials in India should be registered

cards.front: Name ways industry sponsorship creates conflicts of interest in drug evidence.
cards.back: Phase 2 and 3 trials that compare the new drug only with placebo; small, poorly designed post-marketing studies; delayed or withheld publication of unfavourable results; sponsored courses and CME; grants to expert panel members.

cards.front: Short note: Academia-industry interaction in drug development

points: Discovery needs large genomic and proteomic data that one group cannot handle
Academia and industry together improve exploration and development of medicines (Sarkar)
Consortia of academia, industry, foundations and government take part in drug development (Harrison)
Foundations fund drugs for neglected or rare diseases
The Orphan Drug Amendment of 1983 gives incentives for rare-disease drugs (Katzung)
Conflicts of interest: industry-funded approval processes, paid expert panels, sponsored studies, CME, free samples
Negative results may stay unpublished, which exaggerates benefit
Independent ethics committee review and sound trial design

cards.front: Essay: Multicentric clinical trials

points: Trial run at more than one centre by several investigator teams, sometimes across countries
Phase III trials are generally multicentric; phase II often uses 2-4 centres (KDT8)
More patients recruited in less time
Results apply to a wider population, including several countries and ethnic groups
Meets the regulatory needs of several countries
Adds credibility to the trial
Large phase III trials are difficult to design and run, and are expensive (Katzung)
Large volumes of data must be collected and analysed (Katzung)
Every trial needs independent ethics committee approval under GCP (KDT8)
The IRB at each facility must approve the scientific and ethical plan (Katzung)
Institutions doing biomedical research must have an ethics committee (NDCT Rules 2019)

cards.front: What compensation information must a trial subject receive?
cards.back: Subjects must be told whether compensation is provided for physical injury, and in what circumstances. If a subject dies, dependants are entitled to material compensation, and the right to compensation cannot be waived.

cards.front: Essay: Biomedical ethics principles and informed consent in trials

points: Autonomy: freedom, dignity and confidentiality; right to join or leave a trial (KDT8)
Beneficence: act for the subject's and society's good (KDT8, Harrison)
Non-maleficence: do not put the subject at undue risk; first do no harm (KDT8, Harrison)
Justice: fairness, honesty and impartiality in obtaining and reporting data (KDT8)
Written informed consent is required (KDT8)
Subjects must be told of the investigational status and the risks, and may decline (Katzung)
Shared decision-making with the patient (Harrison)
Subjects must be told about compensation for injury (Bennett)
No owner-book passage on consent in children was found, so this part is not written. Check the NDCT Rules and ICMR guidelines

cards.front: Essay: Phase IV studies: objectives, design and conduct

points: Studies after marketing approval, to monitor safety and efficacy in general use (KDT8, Katzung)
Some authors call it post-marketing surveillance, but the two differ (Sarkar)
Real-life performance and factors that change the drug's effect
Safety in special groups such as children and pregnant women
Rare and long-term effects, drug interactions, morbidity and mortality
Added therapeutic benefit and new uses (KDT8)
Large, multicentre and multinational study under the approved indication and population
Much larger samples than earlier phases; structured data from practising physicians (KDT8)
May be interventional or observational (Sarkar)
Protocol approved by the licensing authority (Sarkar)
Low-incidence effects (e.g. 1 in 10,000) appear only with large exposure (Katzung)
No fixed duration (Katzung)
See the PSUR short note

cards.front: Short note: Periodic safety update report (PSUR)

points: Filed by the marketing authorisation holder during post-marketing surveillance
Gives safety data on the new drug in a proposed format (Sarkar)
Every 6 months for the first 2 years
Then annually for the next 2 years
Drug stays in new-drug status for 4 years (Sarkar)
Surveillance can reveal serious effects; some drugs, e.g. rofecoxib, were withdrawn from the market (Sarkar)
The NDCT Rules PSUR clause was not found in the owner's NDCT PDF; this card cites Sarkar. Owner to verify

cards.front: What is ecopharmacology?
cards.back: Study of how pharmaceuticals and personal-care products reach the environment and affect the ecosystem. Coined by Halling Sorensen in 1998; it covers gene, drug and toxin interactions with the environment.

cards.front: What is ecopharmacovigilance (EPV)?
cards.back: Detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing harm that medicines cause in the environment. The term was coined by Velo. Its hardest part is detecting environmental signals and proving cause and effect.

cards.front: Short note: Ecopharmacology and its importance for pharmacovigilance and the environment

points: Effect of pharmaceuticals and personal-care products on the environment and ecosystem
Broad term: covers any entry of these chemicals at any dose or route; pharmaco-environmentology covers only therapeutic-dose effects after excretion
Patient excretion through sewage
Flushing unused or expired drugs
Manufacturing effluent
Sludge, landfill leachate and irrigation with waste water
Diclofenac linked to vulture deaths in the Indian subcontinent
Ethinylestradiol feminising male fish
Propranolol reducing egg production in medaka fish
Antidepressants making lobsters aggressive
Ecopharmacovigilance extends PV to environmental adverse effects
Hardest step: signal detection in the environment and proof of cause and effect
Environmental risk assessment is required before launch, but no set protocol exists for monitoring after launch
Rational use and return programmes for unused drugs
Advanced effluent treatment and green chemistry
Sorting drugs by category, then matching disposal (e.g. high-temperature incineration)

cards.front: Name two drugs found in Indian water bodies
cards.back: Ciprofloxacin in a stream at Patancheru (Hyderabad), and carbamazepine in the Kaveri river near Tiruchirapalli.

cards.front: What is translational research?
cards.back: Turning basic biomedical findings into clinical care, and feeding clinical experience back to the lab. It runs bench to bedside (discovery to patient) and bedside to bench (feedback that improves the discovery).

cards.front: Short note: Translational research in drug development

points: T1: bench to bedside, a basic discovery applied in the clinic
T2: bedside to practice, evidence that the clinical benefit is real
T3: evidence turned into guidelines for health practice
T4: real-world outcome studies
Find the origin and mechanism of disease, including biomarkers
Develop new diagnostic and therapeutic tools
Shorten the time to new drugs
Plan PK and toxicokinetic studies in trials to improve their chance of success
Basic research and molecule design, with physicochemical study
Preclinical PK, PD, toxicity and safety in animals
Link animal findings to early trials in healthy volunteers
Use early-trial data on dose, safety and efficacy to frame clinical guidelines
Closes the gap between what we know and what we practise
In vitro: faster and cheaper; in vivo: whole organisms, better for overall effect; in silico: computer simulation

cards.front: How does a prevention trial differ from a treatment trial?
cards.back: A treatment trial tests a therapy in people who already have the disease. A prevention trial tests how to stop a disease or its recurrence in people who do not have it, with or without risk factors.

cards.front: Short note: Preventive versus therapeutic trials

points: Tests a novel therapy, drug combination, surgery or radiotherapy strategy
Patients randomised to the new intervention or to placebo or standard care
Outcome compared after a set period
Aims to stop a disease or its recurrence in a population
Agents may be medicines, vitamins, minerals or lifestyle changes
Participants do not have the disease
Diagnostic: compares a better test or tool; participants usually show signs
Screening: finds disease in people without symptoms; asks whether it saves lives and at what cost

cards.front: Which authority approves a clinical trial in India?
cards.back: The DCGI, within the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO), decides on the sponsor's trial application (IND). Ethics committee approval and DCGI approval both must come before the trial starts.

cards.front: Short note: Regulatory and ethical bodies in clinical trials

points: Sponsor applies through an IND application
DCGI decides within 90 working days
Indigenous product: approved if no query within 30 days
A rejection can be reconsidered within 60 days
Trial must not begin until the ethics committee and DCGI approve
Investigator undertaking: a legal document committing the investigator to the protocol, filed with CDSCO
IAEC approval needed before toxicity testing or tissue collection
CPCSEA, a statutory body under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960, oversees registration and experiments
New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019

cards.front: What does a brand-name new drug application rest on?
cards.back: Chemistry, manufacturing, controls, labelling and inspection data. A generic product's application (ANDA) instead relies on bioequivalence.

cards.front: Short note: Prerequisites of a new drug application (NDA)

points: Animal pharmacology and toxicology showing the product is reasonably safe for humans
Any earlier human experience with the drug, including use abroad
Chemistry: composition and manufacturer
Manufacturing and stability information
Controls used on the drug substance and drug product
Phase I to III data on safety and efficacy
Phase III randomised trials give the definitive efficacy assessment against standard therapy
Labelling
Inspection of the manufacturing facility
NDA is the full approval route for new and repurposed drugs

cards.front: What is ELISA used for?
cards.back: Detecting and measuring a specific antigen or antibody in a sample. It serves as a diagnostic tool, a quality-control method and an analytical tool in research.

cards.front: Short note: ELISA in pharmacological research

points: Specific antigen-antibody binding gives specificity
An enzyme-labelled detector with a chromogenic substrate gives a colour change, which gives sensitivity
Enzyme usually alkaline phosphatase or horseradish peroxidase
Coat the wells with antigen
Block unbound sites to prevent false positives
Add primary antibody, then enzyme-linked secondary antibody
Add substrate and read the colour by absorbance
Detects antibody in a sample, in two binding steps
Secondary antibody cross-reaction can give non-specific signals
Quantifies antigen or antibody
Screens hybridoma clones for specific antibody production

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacoepidemiology: methods, applications and limitations

points: Study of drug uses, interactions and side effects in a defined population
Looks at how drug effects vary between individuals and between populations
Case and spontaneous reports to flag signals
Case reports are strongest when the event is rare, close in time, has few other risk factors and the drug gives a large excess risk
Observational studies using routine clinical or insurance data (real-world data)
Postmarketing controlled trials
Quantitative disproportionality analysis of spontaneous-report databases
Optimise drug use
Inform regulators' licensing decisions
Study compliance and real-life use
Identify new drug safety problems
Spontaneous reports lack a true denominator, so they cannot give incidence
Disproportionality methods rely on assumptions that are hard to verify
Observational studies are costly and slow, and need database access and data cleaning
Signals from spontaneous reports nearly always need further evaluation
FDA Sentinel System: expanded the FDA ability to run large, rapid observational studies

cards.front: What are the 3Rs of animal research?
cards.back: Replacement, reduction and refinement, defined by Russell and Burch. A fourth R, rehabilitation or responsibility, was added later.

cards.front: Short note: Alternatives to animal experiments in drug development

points: Animals differ in anatomy, metabolism and cell biology from humans
Animal-safe drugs can still harm humans: thalidomide caused limb defects in people, though rodents were not affected
About 94 per cent of drugs that pass animal tests fail in human trials
Absolute replacement: no animals, e.g. in vitro methods
Relative replacement: only animal cells or tissues
Most replacement methods are in vitro
In vitro: faster, cheaper, with fewer ethical and safety concerns
In vitro can mislead: some drugs metabolised in the liver in vivo are not seen in vitro
In silico: computer simulation to speed discovery
Use fewer animals
Limit repeat surgery on one animal to what the protocol and IAEC allow

cards.front: What is the IAEC and which guideline does it follow?
cards.back: The Institutional Animal Ethics Committee, set up in every CPCSEA-registered establishment. It follows CPCSEA guidelines and must approve animal toxicity testing or tissue collection before it starts.

cards.front: Short note: Roles of the IAEC under CPCSEA guidelines

points: CPCSEA is a statutory body under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960
Over 665 laboratories are registered with CPCSEA, and each has an IAEC
Approves protocols before toxicity testing
Approves multiple surgical procedures on one animal only when the protocol specifies them
Members check humane and ethical aspects of each proposal
Aim: reduce animal numbers, minimise sacrifice and avoid repetition
Held at intervals set by the IAEC SOP; expedited review allowed
Researchers may be asked to clarify; independent experts may be consulted
Decisions minuted, with the chairperson's written approval and member signatures
Knows CPCSEA guidelines and the 4Rs
Reads the proposal before the meeting

cards.front: How does WHO define a counterfeit medicine?
cards.back: A product deliberately and fraudulently mislabelled for its identity or source. It may have wrong ingredients, none, too little, or fake packaging, and can be branded or generic.

cards.front: Short note: Substandard and falsified medicines: impact and mitigation

points: Unexpected reactions, toxicity, anaphylaxis or treatment failure
Deaths reported in Africa and Asia
Inert antibiotics fail to cure; fake vaccines give no protection
Disease spread and antibiotic resistance from improper treatment
Counterfeits in the legal supply chain make national treatment irrational
About US$46 billion lost each year by manufacturers
Undermines generic uptake: about 90 per cent of India's drug market is branded generics
Patients and the health system bear the cost of adverse reactions
Public and professional awareness
Mass serialisation: machine-readable serial codes for track and trace
Forensic markers, cloud data repositories and blockchain in supply chains
Stronger law: Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, section 17B, amended 2008
More CDSCO staff and resources, which are limited

cards.front: Essay: Conducting a clinical trial of a new drug (antiepileptic example)

points: Animal pharmacology and toxicity showing reasonable safety for humans
IAEC approval for animal work under CPCSEA guidelines
IND application to the DCGI; decision within 90 working days
Ethics committee approval before the trial starts
Investigator undertaking and commitment to obtain informed consent
First-in-human study in healthy volunteers for safety, tolerability and PK
Dose escalation from a low starting dose
Explores therapeutic efficacy in patients
Phase IIb is definite dose finding: optimum dose with minimal side effects
Randomised controlled trials in large groups against standard therapy
Definitive efficacy assessment; side effects monitored
Real-life performance, factors that change drug effect, and safety in special populations
Post-marketing surveillance and periodic safety update reports
